# What is fitted and why

The scenarios need three data-determined inputs: the current growth rate, the current incidence, and the date transmission changed. Case counts cannot identify the natural history, the baseline delay or the isolation effectiveness $\epsilon$; these are fixed (latent period 6.3 d, infectious period 7 d, baseline delay 7 d, $\epsilon=0.8$) and varied afterwards. The fitted quantities are the starting incidence $i_0$ (on 2 May 2026), transmission rates $\beta_1,\beta_2$ before and after a change date $t_c$, and the negative-binomial dispersion $k$ (counting $t_c$, five parameters, against three for constant transmission).

# Data

Fit B (primary): confirmed cases by report date, 2 June--12 September (96 report intervals) from the BVDOutbreakSize streams [@bvdoutbreaksize2026]. The 22 July harmonisation step (369 reported, 97 new) is replaced by the printed 97, removing 272 retrospective cases. Fit A (cross-check): confirmed cases by onset date from SitRep 121 (25 May--6 September, 105 days; about `\shareOnset{}`{=latex} of confirmed cases have a recorded onset), corrected for right-truncation. Suspected cases, bed capacity and treatment-centre streams stop or change definition and are not used.

# Reporting-delay correction

Each SitRep republishes the onset curve, so the share of an onset day's final count visible $L$ days later can be measured over `\nVintages{}`{=latex} vintages (final = counts at least 28 days old in the latest vintage). A Weibull cumulative distribution $c(L)=1-\exp\{-((L+0.5)/s)^\kappa\}$ fits it: half of cases visible after `\delayHalf{}`{=latex} days, 90% after `\delayNinety{}`{=latex} days, mean `\delayMean{}`{=latex} days. This explains the apparent collapse of the onset curve in the last three weeks (Fig. @fig-fit a,b).

# Model, likelihood and estimation

Model `\eqref{eq:m}`{=latex} is the SEIQR system with $\lambda=\beta[I+(1-\epsilon)Q]/N$:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\dot S=-\lambda S,\;\dot E=\lambda S-\sigma E,\;\dot I=\sigma E-(\tau+\gamma)I,\;\dot Q=\tau I-\gamma Q,\;\dot R=\gamma(I+Q).\label{eq:m}\end{equation}
```
Symptomatic incidence is $i(d)=\sigma E(d)$. Observations are negative binomial with mean $\mu$ and variance $\mu+\mu^2/k$. In Fit A, $\mu_d=c(L_d)\,i(d)$. In Fit B the expected count over a report interval is the incidence convolved with the daily delay probabilities $c(L)-c(L-1)$ and summed over the interval's days. The transmission rate changes from $\beta_1$ to $\beta_2$ on day $t_c$. Maximum likelihood used Nelder--Mead from several starts; $t_c$ was profiled on a 5-day grid and refined to 1 day. Uncertainty draws sample $t_c$ with weights proportional to the profile likelihood and the other parameters from the Hessian-based multivariate normal at that $t_c$. $\Delta$AIC compares with constant transmission.

# Results

```{=latex}
\relax\begin{table}[H]\centering\scriptsize\caption{Fitted parameters (median and 95\% uncertainty interval), $\epsilon=0.8$, baseline delay 7 d; growth rates per day.}
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{../results/tables/fit.tex}}\end{table}
```
A change in transmission was strongly supported ($\Delta$AIC `\fitAdAIC{}`{=latex} for Fit A, `\fitBdAIC{}`{=latex} for Fit B). In Fit B growth fell from `\fitBrBefore{}`{=latex} to `\fitBrAfter{}`{=latex} per day around `\fitBtc{}`{=latex} (interval `\fitBtcRange{}`{=latex}), i.e. $\Rt{}$ from `\fitBReBefore{}`{=latex} to `\fitBReAfter{}`{=latex}. The model incidence on 12 September was `\fitBincEnd{}`{=latex} per day (Fit A: `\fitAincEnd{}`{=latex}, covering only cases with an onset date).

# Diagnostics

95% negative-binomial predictive intervals covered `\fitAcover{}`{=latex} (Fit A) and `\fitBcover{}`{=latex} (Fit B) of observations; lag-1 residual autocorrelation was `\fitAacf{}`{=latex} and `\fitBacf{}`{=latex}. Refitting Fit B at the four corners of the natural-history ranges changed the post-change growth rate only between `\nhRMin{}`{=latex} and `\nhRMax{}`{=latex} per day and the 12 September incidence between `\nhIncMin{}`{=latex} and `\nhIncMax{}`{=latex} (Table `\ref{tab:nh}`{=latex}), so these two quantities are determined by the data rather than by the assumed natural history. Because $\beta$ and $\epsilon$ are not separately identifiable, the growth rates are identical for every $\epsilon$ (Table `\ref{tab:eff}`{=latex}). Testing expanded from `\testsJun{}`{=latex} to `\testsSep{}`{=latex} samples per day while positivity fell from `\posJun{}`{=latex}% to `\posSep{}`{=latex}% (Table `\ref{tab:pos}`{=latex}), so the plateau is not simply a laboratory-capacity ceiling.

# Out-of-sample check

A forecast using data to 12 September overestimated the next 46 days by `\valErrLong{}`{=latex} (model `\valModLongCI{}`{=latex} against `\valObsLong{}`{=latex} observed; observed inside the interval), and the next 15 days by `\valErrShort{}`{=latex} (outside). A constant-rate benchmark erred similarly (`\valNaiveErrLong{}`{=latex} at 46 days).
